title: Big-O Out Loud & Making Code Fast

scenes.say: An interviewer shows you this loop: what's the Big O? Then a script takes half a second. By the end, you'll answer the first in ten seconds, and fix the second.

lines.text: for i in range(n): for j in range(i)

scenes.say: Today you'll do three things. Say any loop's Big O in ten seconds. Spot the hidden costs. And profile slow code, then fix the biggest cost.
lines: Say any loop's Big-O in 10 seconds.
Spot the hidden costs in a loop.
Profile slow code, fix the biggest cost.

scenes.title: Big-O of a nested loop
scenes.statement: Given a loop over n items, say its time complexity out loud, step by step.

example.input: for i in range(n): for j in range(i), n = 5

scenes.note: They want the method, not a guess
scenes.say: Here's the problem. A nested loop, and the Big O? For example, i runs to n, j runs to i, n of five. The answer: ten steps, so O of n squared. They want the method.

scenes.head: Phone book: a million pages
scenes.say: Why Big O exists. Find a name in a million-page phone book. Read every page: a million steps. Open the middle and discard half, again and again: twenty steps. Jump through an index: one step. Big O names that growth.

scenes.head: Say it the same way, every time
scenes.say: Interviewers don't want a memorized table. They want to hear you count. Name n, the input size. Count the loops. Multiply nested ones, add sequential ones. Keep the biggest term and drop constants.
rows: n is the length of the list
inner runs i times, at most n

scenes.head: Trace it: n = 5
scenes.say: Let's trace the nested loop. Five items, so n is five. The inner loop runs i times. When i is zero, it runs zero times. When i is one, once. Then twice. Then three. Then four. Add them up: zero, one, three, six, ten. That is n times n minus one, over two.

scenes.head: The same loop in Python
scenes.say: Here is that loop. Steps starts at zero. The outer loop runs five times. The inner loop runs up to i times. Each pass adds one. It prints ten. For a thousand items it would be near half a million. Drop the one half: constants don't change how cost scales. So O of n squared.
Your turn. Two loops, one after the other. Each runs n times, with no nesting. What is the Big O? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Two separate loops, each n times, one after the other. Big-O?

scenes.head: Add sequential, multiply nested
scenes.say: O of n. Sequential loops add: n plus n is two n, and we drop the two. Nested ones multiply instead. A loop that halves its range is O of log n. That answers our problem.

scenes.title: Why is this loop not O(n)?
scenes.statement: This single loop looks linear, yet it crawls on big lists. Find the hidden second loop.

example.input: for x in items: if x in big_list

scenes.note: items has n entries, big_list has m
scenes.say: Here's the next problem. One loop, and it crawls. For example, for x in items, check x in a big list. The answer: O of n times m in the worst case, not O of n. Items has n entries, the big list has m.

scenes.head: Looks linear. Is it?
scenes.say: Let's solve it. One loop, so most candidates say O of n. Where's the second loop? It hides in the word in. On a list, in scans every element, up to m of them. The real cost is O of n times m.

scenes.head: Hidden costs to know
scenes.say: Four costs hide inside innocent lines. Sorting costs O of n log n. Inserting at the front of a list shifts everything: O of n. Append is amortized O of one: rare resizes, averaged out. A set lookup is O of one on average.
Predict. Ten thousand ids, zero up. We look for the last one, first in a list, then in a set. How many comparisons each?
scenes.q: Checking 9999 in 10,000 ids: comparisons for list vs set?

scenes.head: One lookup, worst case
scenes.say: Here we count comparisons for one lookup. The list scans from the front, all ten thousand, because the match is last. The set hashes to a slot and jumps there: one. Ten thousand times less.

scenes.head: How fast each class blows up
scenes.say: Here we count steps for each class, at a hundred items. Logarithmic, like binary search: about seven. Linear: a hundred. Sorting, n log n: about six hundred sixty. Quadratic: ten thousand. That answers it: a hidden loop.

scenes.title: Why is this script slow?
scenes.statement: A script is slow and you don't know why. Find the cost before you touch anything.
scenes.note: Which part is slow? Measure it.
scenes.say: Last problem, and a different kind. A script checks ten thousand ids against a list. For example, it takes half a second. The goal: under five milliseconds. No guessing which part is slow.

scenes.head: A slow commute
scenes.say: Your commute takes an hour. You time each part. Walking, five minutes. Traffic, fifty. Parking, two. Buying a faster car won't help. You fix the traffic. A profiler is that stopwatch for code.

scenes.head: Ask the profiler
scenes.say: Here is a script that takes half a second. Don't guess. Run it under c Profile, sorted by cumulative time, calls included. The report says hits owns about half a second. Load costs nothing. So hits is the only place worth touching.

scenes.head: Fix: list to set
scenes.say: The cause: seen is a list, so every x in scans it. That's O of n squared overall. Build a set once, and each check is O of one on average. Same answer. Half a second becomes under two thousandths. The price: the set takes O of n extra memory. Say both time and space.

panels.label: before

panels.code:
def hits(ids, seen):
    seen = set(seen)
    return [x for x in ids
            if x in seen]
panels.label: after

setup.bench.py:
import time
ids = list(range(10_000))

def hits_list(ids, seen):
    return [x for x in ids if x in seen]

def hits_set(ids, seen):
    seen = set(seen)
    return [x for x in ids if x in seen]

for f in (hits_list, hits_set):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    f(ids, ids)
    print(f.__name__, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 4), "s")

scenes.say: One more. Hits owns nearly all the time. A teammate makes load ten times faster. How long does the script take now?
scenes.q: hits takes ~99% of the time. You make load 10× faster. Total time?

scenes.head: Speed up the wrong part
scenes.say: About the same. The chart times the whole script, before any change. Load was nothing, so ten times faster saves nothing. Fixing hits drops it to under two.

scenes.head: The loop to repeat
scenes.say: That's our answer to the problem. Measure on realistic input. Fix the biggest cost, algorithm first. Measure again. After algorithms, look at I O: fewer database calls, caching, batching.

scenes.head: Say it in 25 seconds
scenes.say: Big O of this code? I name n, count loops, and keep the biggest term. Best or worst? I give worst, then best. Why drop constants? They don't change scaling. Amortized? The average over many calls. Better? I trade space for time, with a set. Common mistake? Missing a hidden cost, or not stating space.

scenes.head: Optimize slow code, aloud
scenes.say: To optimize slow code, I measure first, with a profiler on realistic input. Then I fix the algorithm, because tweaks give maybe two times. Then I measure again, and only then cut I O, like database calls. The classic mistake is guessing.

scenes.head: Try these this week
scenes.say: Three exercises. Time a nested loop at n of one thousand and two thousand, and watch it quadruple. Profile one of your own scripts. Swap a list lookup for a set and measure.
rows: Time a nested loop at n = 1000, 2000
Run `python -m cProfile` on your own script

scenes.say: So say this. Name n, count loops, keep the biggest. State space too, and watch hidden costs, like in on a list. Measure before you fix.
